paragraphs.text: The tongue that spoke before me has shown us the rays of the cross, and it did so well and wisely. It proclaimed the cross: a slight thing in word, but great in power. It proclaimed the cross, at which unbelievers laugh and before which demons tremble. It proclaimed the cross, which the Jews set up and the whole world has worshipped. It also showed the cross's rays, for it put forward shining virginity as the rays of the cross. That virginity did not just happen to shine; it displayed its beauty by design. Hear how. The cross found the world given over to fornication and made it a world of chastity in the sight of all. The rays of the cross are not proclaimed by words; they are explained by deeds. The cross has no need of a persuasive tongue or an explaining speech. It needs a grateful soul that carries out works of righteousness. Ever since the cross was set up, drunkards have fasted. Ever since the cross was set up, fornicators have become heralds of piety and chastity. Ever since the cross, tax collectors have been shown to be evangelists, and persecutors heralds of piety. Ever since the cross was set up, paradise has stood open. The prophetic word also went on to recall the cross and its root. The root of the cross is virginity: the virgin who bore the one who suffered. She gave birth not by the law of nature but by the power and working of nature's Craftsman. So do not demand a husband in the case of the virgin, or you will be asked for a woman in the case of Adam. If you say, "How did the virgin give birth without a man?", I will answer, "How did Eve come forth from Adam without a woman?" But why must we compare one body with another? Who is the Jew who fights against this? Let him be ashamed, because he reads and recognizes nothing. Do you doubt how the virgin gave birth? Then explain how the rock gave birth to water when it had no vein beneath it, no river spread out under it, no spring of waters. Here is the marvel. The rock was dry and barren, and the rod was dry and barren. A barren rod touched a barren rock and brought forth water. The power of the Most High overshadowed the virgin, and that power is itself alive with immortal life. When it touched living flesh, did it not bring forth fruit, just as the rock brought forth water? In fact, even then it was neither the rock that brought forth the water nor the rod that struck it. It was the power of God, seen through them. The rock was only what appeared to the eye. Or rather, what appeared was a rock, but what was understood was Christ. Paul explains that that rock was an image of Christ: "For they drank," he says, "from a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ." The rock bore the figure of the Master; the rod bore the figure of the cross. This very story explains the power of the cross. Moses struck the rock once and then a second time. If the rock obeys the power of God, what need is there of a second blow? But if Moses strikes apart from the power of God, then neither a second, nor a tenth, nor a hundredth blow can give a barren nature a fruitful one. If the work had simply been God's, without the mystery of the cross, one blow would have been enough; a nod would have been enough; a word would have been enough. But Moses struck once and a second time to show how the grace of the cross is revealed, and that Christ does not let his kindness gush forth unless he is seen through the cross. He did not strike along the same line twice; he traced a cross. He struck once and a second time. Why once and a second time? So that even lifeless nature might revere the sign of the cross. Think of what happens when the emperor is absent. The emperor's image fills the emperor's place. Officials venerate it, sacred new-moon festivals are celebrated, officials go out to meet it, and peoples bow down. They are not looking at the wooden panel but at the emperor's likeness, which is seen not in his own nature but conveyed in the painting. If the image of a mortal king has such power, could not the cross, the image of the immortal King, split a rock just by appearing, and heaven too, and the whole world? Or have you not heard how blessed David questions creation? Moses struck the sea with a rod, struck the rock with the same rod, and worked every sign through that rod. So David questions creation: "What ails you, O sea, that you fled? And you, O Jordan, that you turned back?" What has happened, he asks, that the boundaries of nature have been changed? Why have the foundations of creation been shaken? "What ails you, O sea, that you fled?" Through so many ages you kept your form. The flowing rivers never drove you out of your deep. You never gave way before so many streams. Whom did you see now, that you drew back in awe? Why did you withdraw? Why did you break the boundary set by the Lawgiver, who commanded you, "Thus far you shall come, and you shall not pass beyond"? He set an everlasting law for the sea, and it shall not pass beyond it. If you received such a law, why do you split your waters? What ails you? What has happened? What did you see? What did you suffer? "What ails you, O sea, that you fled? And you, O Jordan, that you turned back? You mountains, that you skipped like rams, and you hills like lambs of the flock?" He asked, and lifeless creation obeys and answers: "Before the face of the Lord." Which face? What face did you see in the sea? What face did you see in the rock? You saw Moses and a rod. No face appeared. Nor did Scripture say, as it usually does, that the Lord appeared in the sea and the Egyptians saw him and were afraid. There was only Moses, holding the rod. Yet creation says: "Before the face of the Lord the earth was shaken." "Before the face of the Lord." Which Lord? The one "who turned the rock into pools of water." Creation calls the rod the face of the Lord, because it bore the image of the Crucified. Hear how the prophet David sketches in another figure that the rod of Moses is an image of our Savior: "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet. The Lord will send forth for you a rod of power from Zion: rule in the midst of your enemies." Do you see that that rod was an image of the rod of power? When he says "rod of power," he means the token of the royal sceptre: "A rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom." "Rod of power" means a powerful kingdom. Why powerful? Because it achieves things through their opposites. Through suffering it grants us freedom from suffering. Through death it gives immortality. Through the cross it crucifies the demons. Through the rod's appearing it led the army of demons in triumph. It is rightly called a "rod of power," then, because it does not win by the usual means; it prevails over its enemies through their opposites. "Before the face of the Lord the earth was shaken, who turned the rock into pools of water." Oh, the ingratitude of the heretics! The rock saw the rod and drew back in awe. The rock saw an image of the cross and was in awe; the heretics saw the Savior himself and did not blush. When the rock saw the image of the cross, it brought forth what it did not have; the heretics saw the Savior and denied what they had received. The rock brings forth what it did not have; these men deny what they received. They received the faith and denied the faith. They received illumination and denied the power of illumination.

But let us come to the physician of our souls. He teaches us by his word and fortifies our city with his relics. I mean John the Baptist, who has washed us today with the word of repentance. Let us watch him teach us the truth through the men he sends to the Savior. Today, as was read in your hearing, John the Baptist sent to our Lord Jesus Christ, asking: "Are you the one who is to come, or do we look for another?" This doubt seems somehow to contradict the prophet's own proclamation. On the surface, the words "Are you the one who is to come, or do we look for another?" belong to someone who has not yet believed and is still searching. So let us question the prophet and forerunner: If you are still searching, how could you bear witness? Why at the baptism did you say, "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world"? Why did you say, "Among you stands one whom you do not know"? And "He who comes from above is above all"? How could you speak to the Savior himself and say, "Lord, I need to be baptized by you"? Are these not your own words: "I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, 'The one on whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining on him, this is he'"? The Father's testimony assured you, the sight persuaded you, you proclaimed it, and those who heard believed. Why then do you lay aside your former knowledge and put on the guise of ignorance? The prophet is not ignorant. He is not ignorant of the Master, whom he worshipped in the womb. He is not ignorant of the Benefactor, whom he pointed out even by leaping. He does not contradict his own words; he is strengthening the convictions of his disciples. For he was in prison. Scripture says that John, being in prison, sent to Jesus. He had been thrown into prison by Herod for rebuking his licentiousness. As a prophet, he saw that his contests had reached their end and that he would soon depart from the world and run to the judge who would award his prize. A great crowd of disciples surrounded him, and many of the Jews thronged about him. He did not want to leave the flock without a shepherd, and he wanted to present those he had taught to the true Teacher. Yet he does not send them to Jesus with the faith and confession he had boldly declared. He did not say, "Since I am departing from the body, go over to Christ, for he is a sufficient Teacher." Testimony given too readily falls under suspicion. But see the marvel. He acted as a prophet, so that he might escape any suspicion about his testimony and also present the truth at work. He sends his disciples to Jesus because he had considered, or rather as a prophet had foreseen, that when the disciples arrived the Savior would be found working miracles. Then, as spectators of the miracles, they would see him in outward form but in truth receive the Savior of the world. It is one thing to bear witness by word, and another to present the truth of the facts. "Go," he says, "ask him and say, 'John the Baptist says.'" He was hinting: I have not forgotten what happened at the baptism. I know whom I baptized: the Redeemer of the world, baptized by me, who myself needed redemption. "John the Baptist says: Are you the one who is to come, or do we look for another?" The disciples came and walked about at the door of the truth. They went to learn, and found the miracles teaching them. For the evangelist says: "In that hour Jesus healed many diseases, cast out many demons, and performed many cures." "In that hour." Which hour? The hour in which John sent them. As a prophet, he timed the sending of his disciples to match the time of the miracles. Then the men who were sent state the purpose of the one who sent them, or rather they repeat his very words: "John the Baptist has sent us, saying, Are you the one who is to come, or do we look for another?" The Savior says: "Go and tell John what you see and hear." He does not say this to send a message to John; he is correcting their thinking. "Go and tell John what you see and hear." There is no need for words. What is needed is eyes as witnesses and a tongue to testify to what the eyes have seen. What shall we say? "The blind see again and the lame walk." Say these things. Say them to him with your tongue; say them to yourselves in your mind. Report them in words to the one who has no need of them. Report to yourselves what you know from the facts. "The blind see again, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the dead are raised, the poor have the gospel preached to them. And blessed is whoever takes no offense at me." Pay close attention. He did not say, "John is blessed if he takes no offense." He knew of no such divided thought in the prophet. He said, "Blessed is whoever takes no offense at me," meaning, "Blessed are you if you take no offense." What does "take no offense" mean? "Blessed are you," he says, "if you do not look at the body you see and deny the Godhead because of it, but learn from the miracles that God is at work in the body." He means that God is at work in the body, but not as he worked in the prophets, nor as he worked in the apostles. He is at work as one who dwells within, is united to it, and takes up into himself what was formed in Adam, that is, humanity.

"The blind see again." What does this have to do with the question "Are you the one who is to come?" They did not ask him, "What are you doing? What do you do? What signs do you make known?" Asked "Are you the one who is to come?", he points to something else: that these are the signs of the one who is to come. How is it clear that these are the signs of the one who is to come? He means: "Since people often disbelieve me, looking at my body and taking offense, let them ask Isaiah, who proclaimed these miracles before they happened." Hear what Isaiah says: "Be strong, you slack hands and paralyzed knees. Take comfort, you who are faint of heart. Be strong, do not fear. Behold our God; behold, the Lord comes with strength." And what does the one who comes do? He opens the eyes of the blind. "Then," he says, "the eyes of the blind will be opened." "Go and tell John: the blind see again." "Then the eyes of the blind will be opened." Set the prophet's words beside the gospel's words, and you will see John, the prophet and forerunner, speaking in harmony with Isaiah. "Then the eyes of the blind will be opened"; "the blind see again." "The deaf hear," and "the ears of the deaf will hear." "The lame walk," and "then the lame will leap like a deer." "And the tongue of stammerers will speak clearly." When did he make the tongue of stammerers speak clearly? A man possessed by a demon, deaf and mute, was once brought to the Lord. What happened? He took him aside privately, spat, and touched his tongue. Why does he who does all things by a word spit? He used spittle as his instrument three times. You find him using this remedy in three miracles. For the man blind from birth, he spat and made clay. For another blind man, he spat on his eyes. For the deaf man with the speech impediment, he spat into his ears. He used this remedy three times, not because he needed it, but to suggest a mystery, since from the beginning the devil had damaged these senses. The woman saw that the tree was good; she saw it with her eye. And she heard the serpent. With which part of her? With her hearing. The serpent's venom ran in through the hearing and through it filled the whole reservoir of the soul. The human being was filled with venom, so that he not only had it but also passed it on. Filled with venom, people were found carrying venom too, for "the venom of asps is under their lips." The serpent shared its bitterness with man, and man passed it on to others. Since the serpent's venom is the serpent's spittle, he brings in spittle against venom as an antidote to the poison. For the naturalists say that what a serpent's venom is to a human being, a human being's spittle is to the serpent. But my spittle drives off the visible serpent, while the Master's drives off the spiritual one. He spits into the ears to wash the venom away. He opens the tongue, saying "Ephphatha," which means "Be opened." What the devil shut through the transgression, the Savior opened through his love for humankind. Then there is the blind man: not the one blind from birth, but another. He took him outside the village, and, the Gospel says, looking up to heaven he sighed, and after sighing he spat on the blind man's eyes. Why does he sigh, and why does he spit? Why does he not give a command as one who has authority? Why does he not heal as God? Why does he look up to heaven and sigh? He does not speak this way from his Godhead. His posture and his utterance show Adam. He had put on the fallen Adam and was called Adam because he took up the nature formed in Adam: "The first man Adam became a living soul; the second Adam became a life-giving spirit." He looked up and sighed in the person of humanity. By that sigh he all but proclaimed the violence of the devil, as if saying: "See how the creature I formed has been outraged! See how the devil's tyranny has choked the organs I fashioned!" He sighed in sympathy with humanity, so fettered by the devil and so held fast by the devil's tyranny. He sighed, and so showed his compassion. Next he shows his power as well. He spits on the man's eyes and lays his hands on him. He spits to wash the venom away. He lays his hands on him to show himself as the Creator. Nothing is formed unless God's hand is laid on it, though it is a spiritual hand. David bears witness to this when he says: "You formed me and laid your hand upon me." He laid his hands on him, and the man regained his sight. The Savior asks him, "What do you see?" He says, "I see people like trees, walking." He had not yet recovered his sight clearly but saw the light dimly. Jesus laid his hands on him a second time, and he saw clearly. Was his power too weak to scatter all the mist at the first touch? Why did the first laying on of the hand show the light more dimly, while the second restored it clearly? It was to explain a mystery. The first formation could not see the truth clearly. That was not because the Craftsman was weak but because the mind was dull. The second birth, regeneration, gave him clear sight. That is why Paul says to this darkened human creature: "You will be darkened through your senseless heart. For claiming to be wise, they became fools." It was not the human creature that was darkened but their senseless heart. And blessed David, preparing the vessel of knowledge for the divine word, says: "Come to him and be enlightened." He laid his hands on him; the man regained sight and says: "I see people like trees, walking." He saw them walking because of the life-force in them, since the human creature moves and goes from place to place. Why does he see them as trees? Because a tree both runs ahead of its season and sheds, and its use is only for a time. After this he does not see them as trees; he sees human beings. The first creature is like a plant that is planted and then uprooted. The second birth shows the human being pure, the same image. And the image of God is not subject to death, for if the image dies, the archetype is insulted. In this way he showed [?] trees [?] his power flashing out through all things.

And it is fitting that he answers with the truth the one who asked only for the sake of appearance. "Tell John what you see and hear: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the dead are raised, the poor have good news preached to them." Where is it said that the poor have good news preached to them? Isaiah did not keep silent about this either: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor." So the question was not one of doubt. It came from someone strengthening his disciples, whose hearts were divided, so that they would not be split over their benefactor but would know the one who had come, and that he had come. But do you ask who it is who came? Do you ask where he came from? Let us inquire. The prophet Habakkuk says: "God will come from Teman." What is Teman? In the Syrian and Hebrew tongue the word means the south. The prophet, as a prophet enlightened by the Holy Spirit, knew that the Savior was to appear to the world from the southern regions, that is, from Palestine. So he says: "God will come from Teman, and the Holy One from a shaded, thickly wooded mountain." What shaded mountain? He calls Zion a shaded mountain, because it was overshadowed by the divine power. And now, I beg you, note what is marvellous here. For at this point a great question arises that needs a great solution. Blessed Habakkuk was explaining the one who came: who the coming one is, and that he is God, and God not known of old, but existing before the ages and revealed at the end of the ages. And the prophet was astonished, for he had received the working of the Holy Spirit. He worshiped God, thinking that the one proclaimed by Moses was God, and that there was no God from God. For a simple faith was given in the beginning: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God, the Lord is one." The prophets measured the saying by its wording, and so they were disposed to worship God, yet without confessing another God, the Son of God. What, then, is made known to the prophet? That the God who is worshiped has a God the Word, who is to be revealed to the inhabited earth and to appear to the world. He does not come into being when he arrives; he exists before the ages and is made known at his coming. What, then, does the prophet say? He heard, and was astonished, that God is made known from God: a new proclamation, a new Word, new in being discovered, not in nature (for "there shall be no new god among you, nor shall you worship a foreign god"). His heart filled with fear, and he begins to sing of the divine coming in the holy song: "Lord, I have heard the report of you, and I was afraid." "You have heard the report of me? Had you not heard before this? Am I not the one who spoke on Mount Sinai? Did I not speak through Moses? Did I not proclaim through the prophets before you? Did not David proclaim?" For Habakkuk came many generations after David. Fourteen generations later he is the one who went to Babylon. For "from David to the deportation to Babylon were fourteen generations," as the Gospel says. If, then, the prophet Habakkuk lived at the time of the Babylonian captivity, Moses and Samuel and Isaiah and Jeremiah and Elijah and Elisha and the greatest of the prophets had already proclaimed God everywhere: "Lord, God of Abraham, Lord, God of Isaac, Lord, God of Jacob, hear me today by fire." Each of the prophets proclaimed God, and it was handed on by hearing. You, prophet, who came after many prophets: this has long been worn familiar by custom. It is already held in the conscience, already held in the mind, already shining beforehand in the conscience of the faithful. Why do you explain it as something strange, and why do you say with trembling, "Lord, I have heard the report of you, and I was afraid"? Where did you hear it, prophet, or who told you? You were wrong to be astonished, and wrong to be afraid. For the one proclaimed brings no fear; he produces the joy of truth and fills us with gladness. "But I," he says, "know what I heard." Where did you hear it? "From God who speaks in me." For God does not speak to the prophets from outside. He is heard within, as an echo in the prophet, and he resounds inside. Where is this shown? Habakkuk himself testifies: "I will stand upon my guard, and I will listen to what the Lord God will say to me." Since I have come upon this subject, I ask you to listen kindly and patiently, so that the meaning does not simply slip past, stripped of its proper contemplation. For we must ask what occasion compelled the word of God. Let the prophet interpret the Savior, or on what subject [?]. For God does not speak idly when there is nothing at hand to speak about. The prophet Habakkuk asked God for teaching. He had nothing to say about the present subject, and he was not yet seeking to speak of the Savior's divinity. Instead he petitioned God about the injustice of human affairs, and showed that life is full of inequity, that injustice holds power, and that greed rules as a tyrant. So he petitions God: "Lord, why have you shown me toils and troubles, to look upon the miseries of men?" It is as if someone were to say: "Why was I born? To be a witness of the evils of the world?" What evil did you see, prophet? "Judgment has taken place before me." That is, they did not respect even the eyes of a prophet. God says to him: "Are you surprised that they do not blush before you? Before me they take bribes and suffer nothing for it [?]." "Judgment has taken place before me, and the judge takes bribes." "The ruler asks, and the judge has spoken peaceable words, the desire of his soul." He does not follow the will of the law but the wish of his own soul. "Therefore the judgment goes forth perverted." Then he says to God: "You who provide for the world and spare all things, do you keep silent while the righteous man is swallowed up by the ungodly? Do you make men like the fish of the sea, which devour one another and have no leader?" When he had made this petition and set these things before God, he finished his speech and began, as a prophet, to say: "I will stand upon my guard, and I will listen to what the Lord will say in me, and what I shall answer to my reproof." See what kind of solution he gives to the questions. He had asked about the injustice of affairs: why does God overlook these things as they happen? "I will stand upon my guard," he says. What is the guard? By "guard" the righteous man means not speaking rashly. When someone, brother, is at a loss over the way things go in life, he ought not to answer rashly: "Does God not provide for the world? Does he not care about what happens? Has he abandoned the inhabited earth? Does he not watch over the land?" David denounces the wicked in this way, saying: "They have humbled your people, O Lord, and afflicted your inheritance; they have killed the widow and the orphan and murdered the stranger; and they said, The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand." They condemned you for lacking providence: "The fool has said in his heart, There is no God," and God does not exercise providence. "But I, the prophet, even if I am vexed at the injustice, do not act rashly." "I will stand upon my guard" means "I do not abandon my guard." What guard? Not to speak rashly, not to pass judgment on things by human reasoning, but to wait for God's teaching. "I will stand upon my guard." By "guard" he means saying nothing rashly. "Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth [?]"; "and I will stand upon my guard, and I will listen to what the Lord God will say in me, and what I shall answer to my reproof." He did not say "what God will answer," but "what I will answer." For both the charges and their resolution come through the same prophet. "And the Lord said to me" (speaking within, not uttering from outside): "Sit down and write clearly on a tablet, in a book, so that the one who reads may run with ease." That is, write in plain letters, distinct and clear, so that difficulty in reading does not hinder understanding: "so that the one who reads may run with ease." What, then, shall I write? "That the one who is coming will come and will not delay." You seek a just judge, one who searches out what the powerful conceal and seeks out sins. You seek a judge who examines what is done and promptly demands an account for everything contrived against the law. So the judge will come: "that the one who is coming will come and will not delay." And he does not say "Behold, I will come," but "Behold, he will come." "I seek you as judge. Who else besides you will be the one coming and judging?" Yet: "the one who is coming will come and will not delay. But the righteous shall live by faith." He does not judge by sight; he stores up the truth by faith. "That the one who is coming will come." Which coming one? "Are you the one who is coming, or should we expect another?" "That the one who is coming will come." Write nothing else. The coming of Christ is the solution of all questions. "The one who is coming will come." Where Christ is, every question is resolved; where Christ is, fear and cowardice are dispelled. Once the disciples were afraid on the sea, and he said: "Take courage, it is I. Do not be afraid." The coming of Christ is the end of all evils. "The one who is coming will come and will not delay. But the righteous shall live by faith." You may believe that the just judge is coming to repay each according to his deeds, and not deny him when you see the apparent delay, but wait for the truth that cannot lie. If so, you will live by faith. The divine apostle takes this saying as referring to the Savior. For we do not devise these interpretations ourselves; we follow our holy fathers and teachers, who interpreted it this way concerning the Savior. For Paul, in his discourse, says: "Holy brothers, partakers of a heavenly calling, hold fast the beginning of your faith." After saying some other things in between, he adds: "For in a very little while the one who is coming will come and will not delay; but the righteous shall live by faith." Then he goes on to explain: "If you shrink back, my soul takes no pleasure. But we, brothers, are not children of shrinking back, but of faith, for the preserving of the soul."

"The one who is coming will come": he will surely come and judge. "Behold, our God repays judgment and will repay; he himself will come." Where his coming is, there too is the judgment. This is the glorious coming, the one still to come, when the angel will sound the trumpet and all who are in the tombs will rise. The prophet heard these things and conversed with God, and he heard of another, a Judge and Master, who was coming. At once he cries out, his mind filled with astonishment, and now he addresses the one who had been proclaimed: "Lord, I have heard the report of you, and I was afraid; I considered your works and was amazed, how you will be known in the midst of two living beings." Many have thought that "you will be known in the midst of two living beings" means between two lives, one of this age and one of the age to come [?]. Many others take it to mean in the midst of two peoples. But in every case the safe interpretation stands firm: between the first covenant and the second. For these are the rational living beings, which give life to us all, since the divine words have life-giving power. "You will be known in the midst of two living beings. As the years draw near you will be recognized; when the time is present you will be shown forth." For you have not yet been recognized; it will happen "as the years draw near." That is, at the fullness of the times you will be made known, and then you will be proclaimed. "This, then, I heard, and I was afraid; I considered your works and was amazed." What works did you consider? That the maker of heaven and earth has been hidden from the world until now. "For he was in the world, and the world came into being through him, and the world did not know him." "As the years draw near you will be recognized; when the time is present you will be shown forth." He did not say "you will come into being"; he did not say "you will be formed," but "you will be known." He is eternal in nature but new in being known. "When the time is present you will be shown forth": that is, you will be proclaimed king. Having said this, he goes on to the dispensation: "Our God will come from Teman" (that is, from the south) "and the Holy One from a shaded, thickly wooded mountain." By "shaded mountain" he means the holy Virgin and Theotokos. Some also take this to mean Mount Zion. For it was overshadowed by the divine power. "His excellence bowed the heavens, and the earth is full of his understanding." Then he begins to talk with him as with a friend and acquaintance: "You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your good ones. You mounted your horses upon the waters of the sea." What horses? The apostles. And by the sea he means the world, as Isaiah says: "Woe, multitude of many nations! Like a surging sea, so shall you be troubled." "You mounted your horses upon the sea, stirring up many waters." The world was filled with turmoil. People heard a new proclamation, a foreign king, a new law and teaching. They were so troubled that when blessed Paul came to Macedonia, the people there cried out: "These men who have turned the world upside down have come here too." Unbelief was troubled, and truth was established. This showed that the same horses could both trouble those who were taken aback and enlighten those who were being sanctified. The one who said "You mounted your horses upon the sea, stirring up many waters" says in the same song: "You will mount upon your horses, and your riding is salvation." Having learned this, the prophet proclaims to the Jews: "Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am doing a work in your days which you will not believe, even if someone tells it to you." Or rather, it runs thus: "Look, you scoffers, and see, and perish; for thus says the Lord: Behold, I am working a work in your days which you will not believe, even if someone tells it to you." By "work" he means the Savior's dispensation. What work, then, am I doing, that when it is proclaimed among you it is not believed? Paul again rightly takes up this saying, and when he is speaking with the Jews in Rome he says: "Beware, then, that what is written does not come upon you: Look, you scoffers, and see, and perish; for I am working a work in your days, a work which you will not believe." But enough of this, so that I may also receive the teaching of the fathers. Let the wounds of the sick be healed. Let them come to the physician, the divine word, which has received the power to heal from God. The scalpel of the word knows how to cut open the sore and to pack the hollows of the wound with the medicines of truth. Physicians, after the incision, put in those rags. They insert them to keep the wound open and stop the sinews from drawing together, and by this packing they prevent the infection from being closed up inside. God does the same: when he has opened the incision with the divine word, as with a scalpel, he then packs it with the divine commandments and the divine teaching. This is not my own idea. Hear the prophet saying to those who had gone astray: "Take words with you and say: Let us return to the Lord our God, for he has struck, and he will heal us; he will strike, and dress the wound, and make you whole." When? "After two days." Why after two days? If it is wholly God's working, it ought to have happened in a single instant. "He will strike, and dress the wound, and make you whole after two days." The reason is that their greatest wound is their fighting against God at the cross, and the healing of those who crucified him is the hope of the resurrection. The Savior rose after two days, on the third, and by rising from the dead he gave the hope of salvation to all who repent. For many tens of thousands of the very men who crucified him believed, as Scripture says: "You see, brother Paul, how many tens of thousands of the Jews who crucified him have believed?" And after the cross, those who had fought against God were healed by the power of the cross. This is why the prophet sets forth the power of the resurrection, saying, "Take words with you." That is: there is no need of deeds, no need to make your defense through actions, but only through words. Since you committed impiety by words, and a word led you into lawlessness, a word will heal you. "Take words with you, and return to the Lord, and say: Let us return to the Lord our God, for he has struck, and he will heal us; he will strike, and dress the wound, and make us whole after two days." How, and in what way? "On the third day we shall rise." And yet it was Christ who rose on the third day, not the rest. Paul explains: "And he raised us up together with him on the third day." We shall rise with him and live before him. To him be the glory and the dominion, with the Father and the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
